metadata.title: Dexmedetomidine‑fentanyl versus propofol‑fentanyl in flexible bronchoscopy: A randomized study

sections.abstract: The aim of the present study was to evaluate the effect of a combination of dexmedetomidine and fentanyl on peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and hemodynamic stability in patients undergoing flexible bronchoscopy. One hundred patients undergoing elective flexible bronchoscopy were randomized into either a propofol-fentanyl group (PF group; n=50) or a dexmedetomidine-fentanyl group (DF group; n=50). SpO2 values, heart rate (HR), systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP and DBP), patients' cough scores and discomfort scores as determined by patients and bronchoscopists, levels of sedation, number of times that additional lidocaine was required, elapsed time until recovery, and adverse events were recorded. The mean SpO2 values in the DF group were significantly higher than those in the PF group (P<0.01), and HR, SBP and DBP were significantly lower in the DF group than in the PF group (P<0.05). There were no statistically significant differences between the two groups in terms of cough scores or discomfort scores, sedation levels, or number of times that additional lidocaine was required (P>0.05). Elapsed time until recovery in the DF group was significantly longer than in the PF group (P=0.002). The incidence of hypoxemia was significantly lower in the DF group than in the PF group (P=0.027), but the incidence of bradycardia was significantly higher in the DF group than in the PF group (P=0.037). Dexmedetomidine‑fentanyl was superior to propofol-fentanyl in providing satisfactory SpO2. Furthermore, dexmedetomidine-fentanyl attenuated hemodynamic responses during bronchoscopy and maintained hemodynamic stability in the early stage of the procedure.
sections.methods: Prospective, randomized, single-center study at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University (December 2013 to May 2014). Adults aged 20-75 years (ASA I-III) undergoing elective flexible bronchoscopy were randomized by computer-generated list to propofol-fentanyl (PF) or dexmedetomidine-fentanyl (DF). All patients received oxygen 4 L/min via nasal cannula starting ≥5 min before fentanyl; if SpO2 <90% for >30 s, oxygen was increased to 6 L/min and airway maneuvers applied. Topical anesthesia: 2% lidocaine to naso/oropharynx; 3-ml aliquots of 1% lidocaine to vocal cords, trachea, main bronchi; supplemental lidocaine as needed. PF group: propofol via target-controlled infusion (Injectomat TIVA Agilia) using a three-compartment model; initial effect-site target 4 µg/ml, then maintained 2-4 µg/ml during the ~12-min loading period; fentanyl 1 µg/kg before sedation. DF group: fentanyl 1 µg/kg before sedation; dexmedetomidine loading 1 µg/kg over ~12 min, then infusion 0.5 µg/kg/h. Adequate conscious sedation indicated by ptosis; if insufficient sedation (pain/discomfort, agitation, persistent cough, inadequate response), give additional 2 ml of 2% lidocaine via bronchoscope. Monitoring: continuous ECG and SpO2; noninvasive BP every 5 min. Timepoints: T1 (1 min before fentanyl), T2 (start bronchoscopy), T3 (1 min after start), T4 (5 min after start), T5 (end). Outcomes: SpO2, HR, SBP, DBP at T1-T5; cough and discomfort VAS (patients and bronchoscopists); MOAA/S at T2 and T4; number of additional lidocaine administrations; recovery time (from scope withdrawal to fully awake and conversant); adverse events (hypotension, bradycardia, hypertension, tachycardia, hypoxemia). AE management: hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <60 mmHg) treated with ephedrine 10 mg; bradycardia (HR <60 bpm) with atropine 0.3 mg; hypertension (SBP >180 mmHg or DBP >100 mmHg) and tachycardia (HR >100 bpm or >20% from baseline) with additional 2 ml of 2% lidocaine into the trachea. Statistics: Repeated-measures ANOVA for SpO2, HR, SBP, DBP over time; Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U for continuous outcomes; χ2, Fisher’s exact, or Mann-Whitney U for categorical data; SPSS v18; two-sided α=0.05. Sample size: n=44/group to detect 3% difference in mean SpO2 (σ=4.3) with 90% power at α=0.05; planned n=50/group allowing 10% dropout.
sections.results: 100 patients randomized: DF n=50, PF n=50; baseline demographics, ASA class, comorbidities, indications, procedure types, and durations balanced. SpO2: no difference at T1 and T5; DF higher than PF at T2 (95.16±2.38 vs 93.60±2.63), T3 (94.80±2.05 vs 93.20±1.83), T4 (93.92±1.64 vs 92.72±1.60); P<0.01 at T2-T4. HR: DF lower than PF at T2 (61.72±3.60 vs 68.28±5.94), T3 (82.24±8.70 vs 89.36±5.68), T4 (80.36±9.26 vs 84.96±8.06), T5 (61.14±11.06 vs 69.28±6.53); P<0.05 at each. SBP: DF lower than PF at T3 (114.92±10.66 vs 125.52±6.65) and T4 (105.72±9.29 vs 115.36±11.90); P<0.05. DBP: DF lower than PF at T3 (80.36±9.26 vs 86.36±5.77) and T4 (75.98±5.27 vs 79.44±6.64); P<0.05. VAS cough and discomfort: no significant differences (data in Figure 5). Additional lidocaine requirement: no difference (P=0.802). MOAA/S at T2 and T4: no difference. Recovery time: DF longer than PF (13.10±1.68 vs 11.91±2.14 min; P=0.002). Adverse events: hypoxemia lower with DF (1/50) vs PF (7/50), P=0.027; bradycardia higher with DF (13/50) vs PF (5/50), P=0.037; no significant differences in hypotension (8/50 vs 5/50), hypertension (5/50 vs 7/50), or tachycardia (6/50 vs 8/50). Willingness to repeat bronchoscopy: similar (38/50 vs 33/50; P=0.271).
